questions.q: What is the best time to ask restaurant guests for feedback?
questions.a: The best time is while the experience is still fresh: right after the meal, at payment or within a couple of hours of the visit. Staff can ask happy tables in person, and a QR code on the receipt or table card works well while guests wait for the bill. A follow-up text or reservation message the same day catches guests who've already left.

questions.q: How do I get more customers to leave reviews?
questions.a: Ask proactively, because most guests only review when they're very happy or very unhappy. Make it easy with a direct link to your review page by QR code, text message or email. Train your team to ask at natural moments, such as after a smooth checkout or when a table compliments the food.

questions.q: What questions should a restaurant feedback survey include?
questions.a: A good survey starts with an overall rating, then asks guests to rate food, service, ambience and value. Add a routing question for dine-in or delivery and a question about which location or app they used. Follow-up questions for low scores, a recommendation question and a short optional demographics section round it out.

questions.q: Should I offer a reward for completing a restaurant survey?
questions.a: A small reward, such as a coupon, discount or loyalty points, gives guests a reason to finish the survey. Mention it on the opening screen so people know it's coming. On the thank-you screen, also promise a follow-up to unhappy guests so they feel heard.

questions.q: How can software help restaurants collect and use guest feedback?
questions.a: Survey software lets you reach guests by text or email, keep surveys short and see results by location. Momos, for example, offers customizable surveys with conditional questions, sends positive responses toward Google reviews and moves negative feedback into an automated customer recovery workflow. Its AI then turns feedback into location-level insights.
